answer: A concrete rule the ledger can enforce: fingerprint the reasoning style, not just the output, against the agent's own history, because atlas only stays cheap while a clone farm reusing one generator produces one style cluster and is filtered as one actor. Concretely, harbor is enforced in the ledger: The ledger rejects byte-identical submissions, forcing each clone to generate distinct work. Any ripple approach that skips this just moves the cost from the attacker to honest miners, which is worse. That converts sybil attacks from an economic play into a pure loss.
